title: Origins and Road to War
sub: The Aouzou Strip and Chad's civil wars draw Libya south

markers.label: Aouzou Strip
markers.description: Libya claimed and occupied the Aouzou Strip, turning a border dispute into a long intervention in Chad.

markers.label: N'Djamena
markers.description: Chad's capital was repeatedly shaped by factional fighting and outside intervention.

slides.title: Border Claim Meets Civil War
slides.cap: A French Sikorsky H-34 in Chad, reflecting the long outside military role in the conflict.
slides.body: The Chadian-Libyan War began where Libya's claim to the Aouzou Strip met Chad's internal fragmentation. Muammar Gaddafi backed Chadian factions, deployed Libyan troops, and tried to shape the central Sahara's politics. Chad's governments and rival armed movements fought each other as well as Libya, which made the war both an international conflict and a civil-war battlefield.

stats.val: Libyan intervention fused with Chadian factional politics

title: Second Battle of N'Djamena
sub: Factional fighting and Libyan-backed power politics

markers.label: N'Djamena
markers.description: The capital became the central prize in Chad's factional struggle and Libya's effort to shape the government.

slides.title: The Capital as the Prize
slides.cap: N'Djamena during the era of Chadian-Libyan conflict.
slides.body: The Second Battle of N'Djamena showed how Chad's civil war and Libya's intervention reinforced each other. Control of the capital meant access to legitimacy, ministries, foreign recognition, and the ability to invite or resist outside troops. Libyan support helped some factions, but it also deepened resistance among Chadians who saw Gaddafi's role as occupation rather than alliance.

stats.val: Capital fighting internationalized Chad's civil war

title: Operation Manta
sub: France draws a line against Libyan advance

markers.label: Manta line
markers.description: French forces deployed south of Libya's zone of influence to deter further advance.

markers.label: N'Djamena air bridge
markers.description: French airpower and logistics helped stabilize the Chadian government.

slides.title: A French Stop Line in the Desert
slides.cap: French forces in Chad during Operation Manta.
slides.body: Operation Manta was France's 1983 intervention to prevent Libya and its Chadian allies from overrunning the south. Paris avoided a full reconquest of the north, but it created a military barrier that protected Hissene Habre's government and bought time for Chad's forces to reorganize. The operation made the war a visible Cold War-era test of French credibility in Africa.

stats.val: Stops Libya from converting northern control into national victory

markers.label: N'Djamena
markers.description: French aircraft and troops helped defend the Chadian government after renewed Libyan pressure.

markers.label: Ouadi Doum
markers.description: Libya's northern air base became a major target as Chad and France pushed back.

slides.title: Airpower, Deterrence, and the Northern Bases
slides.body: Operation Épervier renewed and expanded the French role after Libyan-backed forces crossed the earlier line. French airpower, intelligence, and logistics helped prevent a Libyan breakthrough while Chadian units prepared for a more mobile northern campaign. The intervention did not win the war by itself, but it shaped the conditions that let Chad attack isolated Libyan bases.

title: Toyota War
sub: Chad's mobile campaign breaks Libya's desert army

markers.label: Fada
markers.description: The victory at Fada opened the decisive mobile phase of the war.

markers.label: Ouadi Doum
markers.description: Chadian forces captured the Libyan base and large quantities of equipment.

markers.label: Maaten al-Sarra
markers.description: Chadian raids reached deep into Libya's rear area near the end of the campaign.

slides.title: The Decisive Campaign, Folded Into the Larger War
slides.cap: Visual reference for the mobile Chadian campaign.
slides.body: The Toyota War was the final and decisive phase of the Chadian-Libyan War, not a separate story here. Chadian forces used fast pickup trucks, anti-tank missiles, local desert knowledge, and flexible command to outmaneuver Libya's heavier formations. At Fada, Ouadi Doum, Aouzou, and Maaten al-Sarra, mobility turned Libya's bases into traps. The campaign shattered Gaddafi's position in northern Chad and forced Libya toward a ceasefire.

stats.val: Libyan forces expelled from most of northern Chad

title: Battle of Fada
sub: A mobile Chadian victory opens the endgame

markers.label: Fada
markers.description: Chadian forces destroyed or captured much of a Libyan armored force around Fada.

slides.title: Speed Against Armor
slides.cap: Image selected for the Battle of Fada event.
slides.body: At Fada, Chadian forces demonstrated the method that would define the final campaign. Fast columns struck Libyan armor and fixed positions before heavier units could react effectively. The battle damaged Libyan morale, delivered captured equipment to Chad, and proved that the northern occupation could be broken by mobility rather than matched tank for tank.

stats.val: Chadian mobile tactics defeat heavier Libyan forces

title: International and Human Dimensions
sub: Foreign intervention and civilian strain across the Sahara

markers.label: Paris-N'Djamena axis
markers.description: French support repeatedly prevented Libya from turning battlefield gains into control of Chad.

markers.label: Northern Chad
markers.description: Occupation, raids, and base warfare placed desert communities under prolonged pressure.

slides.title: A Regional War Watched From Abroad
slides.cap: Battle of Fada imagery reflecting the war's final phase.
slides.body: France, the United States, Sudan, and regional governments all read the war through the lens of Libyan expansion. For Chadians, the war meant factional violence, occupation in the north, displacement, and repeated battles around towns and oases. The international dimension mattered because outside airpower and support shaped the battlefield, but the human cost remained local and long-lasting.

stats.val: Civil war, occupation, and intervention overlapped

title: Outcome and Legacy
sub: Libya withdraws and the Aouzou question moves to court

markers.label: Aouzou Strip
markers.description: The disputed strip remained the legal issue after Libya's military defeat.

markers.label: International Court of Justice
markers.description: The ICJ awarded the Aouzou Strip to Chad in 1994.

slides.title: Military Defeat, Legal Settlement
slides.body: Chad's 1987 victories forced Libya to accept a ceasefire and ended Gaddafi's attempt to dominate northern Chad by force. The remaining Aouzou Strip dispute moved from battlefield to law, and the International Court of Justice awarded the territory to Chad in 1994. The legacy is a rare case where a smaller, mobile force defeated a larger expeditionary army and then converted that result into recognized sovereignty.
